Figure 1:Comparison of attention maps produced by the DINOv2 trained model and our trained model. For each model, we show the attention maps averaged over the validation set of the ImageNet-1k(Russakovsky et al., 2015)and the attention maps obtained from a single example image.
Existing learned perceptual representations (left) in individual attention heads often tend to be ambiguous or overly similar within the example image and across images in the dataset, which limits their interpretability.
In contrast, our method (right) selectively steers the focus, leading to the emergence of diverse and spatially focused perceptual capabilities.
(Images: Visualization of 16 attention heads in the last layer of trained ViT-L/16-Reg model)
Figure 2:Overview of our proposed visual focusing loss functionsℒin\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{in}}andℒout\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{out}}.
Figure 3:Comparison of the average of attention maps on ImageNet-1k across four training methods using pretrained models (a)-(d).

Figure 4:Comparison of the average of attention maps on ImageNet-1k from head11to head1616and their head mean.
Each model is trained using one of four loss functions (a)-(d).

Figure 5:An example of attention maps for each model (a)-(d). The image in the top left is the “input”.
The images labeled “mean” represent the head means of the attention maps used as heat maps, and the images labeled “mask” represent the segmentation masks.
Figure 6:Changes in segmentation accuracy at each position compared to the accuracy of the original DINOv2 model.
